card: Explicitly sets accepted sockets for inbound P2P connections and HTTP server clients as non-blocking. On Linux, accepted sockets do not inherit O_NONBLOCK from the listening socket, which could allow a malicious peer to stall the node indefinitely if any send or recv invocation missed the MSG_DONTWAIT flag. The author characterizes this as an inexpensive defense-in-depth safeguard against socket-blocking denial-of-service bugs. It requires no prerequisites.
evidence: PR description: "A mistake here would be critical, as it would allow a malicious peer to stall us indefinitely for free."
Commit baf93e8ffd notes that while Linux does not inherit O_NONBLOCK, "we always send() and recv() with MSG_DONTWAIT", making this an explicit defense-in-depth measure that costs virtually nothing.
problem: Accepted sockets on Linux do not inherit the O_NONBLOCK flag from the listening socket. While existing send and recv calls on POSIX systems mitigate this by setting MSG_DONTWAIT, relying on per-call flags leaves the node vulnerable to remote stalling attacks if any socket I/O call fails to pass the non-blocking flag.

risk.why: A mistake when setting socket options on accepted connections could cause inbound P2P or RPC connections to fail or terminate unexpectedly.

scope_notes: The diff was not provided in the patch data, but metadata reports a small +16/-0 change across two files.
summary: Explicitly marks accepted sockets for inbound P2P connections and HTTP clients as non-blocking immediately upon acceptance. This brings accepted sockets into line with newly created sockets configured via CreateSockOS, ensuring consistent non-blocking behavior across all supported operating systems.
